changeRequests.title: Modernize calendar UI for quick scanning and minimal clicks
changeRequests.description: User wants the calendar to match the modernized Gil wallet approach — less clicks needed to navigate and find events, everything scannable at a glance without hunting around.
changeRequests.details: Designed a mockup first (published as an Artifact) showing an always-visible horizontal week-strip as the primary way to browse days — no more opening a toggle just to see today. Implemented for real in mission-control.html: added #mobWeekStrip above the existing month-grid-behind-toggle (kept, restyled flat, for full month navigation), wired to the existing selectedKey/renderMobDaySummary/renderMobCalQuests functions so day selection stays consistent with the existing data flow. Restyled the toggle button, grid card, and day-event-list rows to Inter/flat per the N26 direction (day-event-dot changed from a small circle to a vertical accent bar). Deliberately did NOT change the quest add-row (rank select, time picker, task input) — that's shared with the Home tab and out of this redesign's scope, so it keeps its existing JRPG look. Deliberately did NOT change month-grid day-cell styling (VT323 grid) to limit risk to the dense date-picker component. Week-strip day taps do not auto-open the day modal (unlike month-grid taps, which keep that existing behavior) — intentional, to match the 'scan quickly' goal.

changeRequests.title: Modernize Gil wallet UI with N26-inspired design
changeRequests.description: User wants the Gil budget tracker tab to feel like a modern banking app with minimal friction and clicks.
changeRequests.details: Designed a mockup first (published as an Artifact) showing balance-first hero + two-tap quick actions + flat transaction list. User approved ('it looks beautiful') then asked to also cover the 4 sub-tabs the mockup didn't show (Trends/Accounts/Bills/Goals) plus the weekly/monthly mode toggle — confirmed via follow-up question to restyle all 5 sub-tabs consistently rather than just the main view. Implemented in mission-control.html, scoped entirely to #mobBudgetView (verified via grep that .bento-tile/.budget-txn*/.budget-tab* classes are exclusive to this tab, so no leak into Home's stats or other tabs): added a balance hero with a real 7-day cumulative-net sparkline and an up/down/flat delta vs last week (both derived from actual transaction data, new weekRangeOffset/weekNetForOffset/gilSparkPoints/buildGilSparkSvg helpers), added two prominent Expense/Income quick-action buttons wired to the existing openMoneyPad() flow (same fast per-card add already shipped, no new transaction-commit code path), gave transaction rows a category-colored icon chip (reusing each category's real BUDGET_CATS color via the existing hexAlpha() helper), and restyled the shared bento-tile/budget-tab/budget-txn/mini-btn/save-field classes to Inter + flat surfaces + tabular-nums, scoped via the #mobBudgetView prefix pattern already established in the codebase — so Trends/Accounts/Bills/Goals inherit the new look automatically without their own render logic changing. No functional behavior was touched (accounts, recurring bills, savings goals, weekly/monthly mode all work exactly as before).

changeRequests.title: Make pending change queue expandable and readable
changeRequests.description: User can't actually see what's queued without opening each tab — they want the pending change queue in Mission Control to show summaries or titles they can read at a glance, and ideally be able to expand/click each one to see the full spec without leaving the app.
changeRequests.details: Investigation found the Change Queue modal already had badge counts, click-to-expand rows, and full spec/implementation-notes display — the real issue was a bug: toggleCqDetail() looked up the row via getElementById(`cqRow-${CSS.escape(id)}`), but CSS.escape() is for CSS selectors, not element ids, and getElementById does a literal string match. Since every request id starts with a digit (the year), CSS.escape numeric-escaped it, so the lookup never matched the real DOM id and the row never visibly expanded. Fixed by using the raw id: getElementById('cqRow-'+id) (mission-control.html).

changeRequests.title: Expand Red's research scope and add communication loop
changeRequests.description: Red currently only does design research for the app itself, but the user wants Red to be able to research anything while maintaining a design focus.
changeRequests.details: Scoped via Q&A with the user before implementing: Mission Control's design stays a secondary lens on any briefed topic (not a full replacement of MC framing); Red got real persistent memory (redMemory, mirroring edMemory's storage pattern with its own rmem- id prefix) and its own tool set (save_red_memory, forget_red_memory, start_red_research); Red's tools are structurally separate from ED's (RED_TOOL_HANDLERS vs ED_TOOL_HANDLERS, never merged) so Red cannot reach queue/task/expense/ED-memory actions — enforced in code, not just prompt text, per the user's explicit boundary: 'ED should be like my personal assistant... Red should be purely for research purposes and will not do it if it falls under ED's scope.' Added a new /api/red-chat endpoint + briefing chat box in the Design Lab modal so the user can brief Red on a topic before it researches. Threaded an openTopic flag through runDesignResearch/buildFindingSchema/runSingleFindingRevision/saveDesignResearchWiki so open-topic runs get a real primary-subject framing (with an optional mc_relevance field noting any genuine tie-back) while the existing MC-focused entry points (manual focus box, daily auto-run) are untouched. Also generalized runChatTurn (previously hardcoded to ED's 6 tools) to accept a toolHandlers map per call, since Red needed to reuse it. Verified end-to-end: ED's existing chat/tools still work identically after the refactor, and a real open-topic research run (desk lamps for eye strain) produced correctly-scoped findings, tags, and wiki content (server.js, mission-control.html).

changeRequests.title: Improve Change Queue UI: Dropdown & Text Readability
changeRequests.description: The change queue dropdown is clunky and hard to use — text is hard to read and opening the dropdown to see queued change details requires too much friction.
changeRequests.details: Redesign the change queue dropdown/modal to improve readability and accessibility.

changeRequests.title: Unified Quest/Calendar Sync with Dual Views
changeRequests.description: User wants quests and calendar events to be deeply integrated so that adding a task creates a calendar event and vice versa, keeping them synced. The quest view should show a filtered, daily-focused UI of today's items (tasks + events combined), while the calendar view shows the full month with all items visible across dates.
changeRequests.details:
**Behavior:**
- When a task is added to quests, automatically create a corresponding calendar event on that date
- When a calendar event is added, automatically create a corresponding task in the quest list
- Both should reference each other so they update/delete together
- Editing one should update the other

**Quest View (Daily):**
- Show today's tasks and calendar events in a unified list
- Display both kinds of items in a single scrollable interface
- Keep the existing quest UI styling but include event items alongside tasks

**Calendar View (Monthly):**
- Show the full month grid as it does now
- Display all tasks and events across all dates in the month
- Both should be visually represented on the calendar tiles

**Implementation notes:**
- Add a `linkedEventId` field to tasks and `linkedTaskId` field to events in localStorage to maintain the sync relationship
- Update `addTask()` and `addDayEvent()` to create the paired item
- Update `deleteTask()` and `deleteDayEv()` to remove both linked items
- Filter quest view to show only today's date using existing date logic
- Ensure calendar rendering includes both event and task data

changeRequests.title: Budget Tracker Overhaul: Vision & Coordination
changeRequests.description: User wants a comprehensive overhaul of the budget tracker that encompasses visual redesign, interaction patterns, data visualization, and gamification — all three coordinating under one vision. The two existing queued items (Coins-for-Log Micro-Rewards and Category Labels on Donut Slices) should be implemented as separate tasks but aligned to serve this overarching vision, not replace it.
changeRequests.details:
This is a coordination spec, not an implementation task yet. Before Claude Code implements any budget changes, read this first:

**Vision:** Transform the budget tracker from a transaction logger into an engaging, gamified financial dashboard that rewards tracking, visualizes spending at a glance, and makes category breakdowns intuitive.

**Scope (all four areas):**
1. **Visual redesign** — Layout, spacing, hierarchy, use of the bento-grid tile system already in the codebase
2. **Interaction patterns** — How users add/edit transactions; quick-add workflows; category selection
3. **Data visualization** — Enhance charts, breakdowns, period comparisons; make data scannable
4. **Gamification** — Micro-rewards (coins-for-logging), progress indicators, streaks, visual feedback

**Alignment with existing queue:**
- `Entry-Level Micro-Rewards: Coins-for-Log` — implement this as specified; it serves the gamification pillar
- `Category Labels on Donut Slices (Enhanced)` — implement this as specified; it serves the visualization pillar

**Implementation order:** Do NOT start until user explicitly approves this vision. When approved, clarify with user whether to run the two existing items first, or whether this vision spec requires changes to them before implementation.

changeRequests.title: Entry-Level Micro-Rewards: Coins-for-Log (Dual Scroll Wheels)
changeRequests.description: Liked this Design Lab finding from Red and queued it for implementation.
changeRequests.details:
Award fractional GIL coins instantly when players log a transaction or check a habit, with reward amount and category selected via two compact side-by-side scroll wheels—no manual input, just spin-to-pick. The amount wheel spans 5.00 down to 0.01 GIL, letting you calibrate rewards by frequency: daily check = 0.10, weekly milestone = 0.50, big win = 2.50. This ties immediate dopamine (coin pop, wallet flash) directly to the act of logging, reinforcing visibility without requiring external motivation.

Source: [Guul Games: Gamification in Habit Tracking Apps](https://guul.games/blog/gamification-in-habit-tracking-apps-examples-and-results)

changeRequests.title: Category Labels on Donut Slices (Enhanced)
changeRequests.description: Liked this Design Lab finding from Red and queued it for implementation.
changeRequests.details:
Place category names directly on the outer edge of each donut slice in high-contrast colored bands with white text, positioned tangent to the slice perimeter. This eliminates the separate legend entirely—users read spending instantly at a glance without cross-referencing. The enhanced label bands use dark backgrounds and bold typography to stand out sharply from the pie chart, making them scannable even on mobile.

Source: [Budget Tracker App UI/UX Design by Cansaas Agency](https://contra.com/p/vk67o2ZR-budget-tracker-app-uiux-design)

changeRequests.title: Auto-reload design revisions in Design Lab
changeRequests.description: Design Lab required manually reopening the slideshow to see revised findings after rating one — no indication a revision had even shipped. This implements auto-reload: the Design Lab list and any open slideshow poll for new research/revisions while open, a small pulsing dot shows live-checking is active, a banner announces a ready revision and cross-fades it in automatically after a few seconds, and a pause button in the slideshow footer lets the user freeze auto-refresh mid-read.
changeRequests.details: Implemented directly in mission-control.html: checkDlListForNewRuns()/checkSlideshowForRevision() poll GET /api/design-research every 10s only while the relevant modal has the .active class; dl-live-dot pulses via CSS animation; new list rows fade in with dl-row-new; #dlRevisionBanner shows on a fresh isRevision run and swaps the #dlSlideshowFrame src with an opacity fade unless _slideshowPaused is true; #dlPauseBtn toggles that flag. No backend changes needed — reuses the existing design-research/rate endpoints.

changeRequests.title: Smart Tile Hierarchy: Variable-Size Cards for Financial KPIs
changeRequests.description: Unlike equal-width card layouts, a bento grid uses tile size to signal importance — hero KPIs anchor in large tiles, category breakdowns sit in smaller secondary tiles, guiding attention without relying on labels alone. Applied to Mission Control's GIL WALLET: the period spent total is now a 2-column hero card with its progress bar, REMAINING is a secondary tile, and per-category spend (food, transport, etc.) renders as small sorted tiles below.
changeRequests.details: Implemented directly in mission-control.html: new categoryBreakdown(txns) computes per-category expense totals (excludes income) sorted descending; bentoCatTilesHtml() renders up to 4 category tiles using existing BUDGET_CATS icons/labels. buildBudgetGilHTML() (desktop) and buildMobBudgetGilHTML() (mobile) both replaced their equal-width SPENT/REMAINING row with a .bento-grid: a .bento-hero tile (period spent + bar) spanning full width, a REMAINING tile, then the category tiles. New CSS classes: .bento-grid/.bento-tile/.bento-hero/.bento-cat/.bento-label/.bento-val/.bento-bar-wrap/.bento-sub, with #mobBudgetView overrides for larger phone type.

designFeedback.findingTitle: Weekly Pattern Heatmap in Cal Tab (Color-Grid Story at a Glance)
designFeedback.findingDescription: Show a small color-coded grid for each quest in the Cal tab's weekly view (green=yes, yellow=skip, red=missed, gray=not-attempted) so users can spot which habits are struggling without opening charts. Inspired by Way of Life's approach: the grid tells the story at a glance, and the color palette fits Mission Control's existing accent scheme. Keep it compact (a small 7-column row per quest) to avoid clutter in an already full calendar view.

designFeedback.findingTitle: Daily Quest Check-In with Skip/Yes Toggle (Forgiving Streak Model)
designFeedback.findingDescription: Distinguish between "skipped" (circumstances, not a choice) and "missed" (chose not to), so one bad day doesn't reset weeks of progress. This directly reduces quit-after-setback behavior documented in Way of Life's design. The visual should show yes/skip buttons on the same row for ultra-fast logging, with skip graying out the entry but keeping the streak chain intact. Matches Mission Control's focus on realistic, grace-based gamification.

designFeedback.findingTitle: Inline Context Notes for Habit Logging (Like Way of Life)
designFeedback.findingDescription: Allow brief 1-2 sentence notes logged alongside quests (especially S-rank items), so users can attach real-world context ("skipped due to travel", "harder than usual") instead of just a binary yes/no. This surfaces patterns over time without punishing streaks. Show notes in a collapsed/expandable format to keep the daily view clean but searchable for weekly reviews. Fits Mission Control's design philosophy of showing only what matters on first glance.

designFeedback.findingTitle: Pause-on-Interact with Manual Refresh Fallback
designFeedback.findingDescription: Provide flexibility: if you're investigating a specific data point and don't want visuals to change, pause live refresh. While paused, no automated refreshes occur; when ready, resume to return to real-time monitoring. A small pause button (⏸) in the slideshow footer stops incoming revisions mid-read; tapping resume or navigating to the next finding auto-restarts polling. Prevents frustration when user is comparing the old mockup to feedback notes. Low-friction, respects user agency—very on-bran

designFeedback.findingTitle: Seamless Fade-and-Replace Slide Transition on Revision
designFeedback.findingDescription: While one box shrinks and gets ready to leave, the next box enters the scene, creating a constant loop of boxes entering and exiting continuously. When a revision loads, fade out the old finding card (200ms) and fade in the new one from behind it. The mockup itself (the HTML sandbox iframe) cross-fades instead of hard-reloading, preserving scroll position if the user is mid-read. Feels alive without breaking JRPG aesthetic; uses Mission Control's accent/green palette for the fade pulse.

designFeedback.findingTitle: Event-Driven Soft Refresh with Connection Status Badge
designFeedback.findingDescription: Detect when data arrives and trigger a refresh only when needed, rather than constant polling. When Red finishes a revision, the server emits a lightweight event; the client polls short intervals only while the slideshow modal is open. A small "●" badge in the modal header animates to signal the refresh is live, never blocking the user's view of the current slide. Pairs well with Mission Control's retro aesthetic via simple dot/pulse animations in the accent color.

designFeedback.findingTitle: Competence Over Points: Mastery-Proof Dashboard Pattern
designFeedback.findingDescription: The gamified productivity category is converging with identity design — not task counts but skill proof. Mission Control could show "competence anchors" (time-of-day proficiency, task-mode synergies, depth vs. speed trade-offs) as contextual mastery evidence tied to historical patterns, replacing generic streak punishment. Systems with great Competence but no Autonomy create a golden cage; the magic happens when all three (Competence, Autonomy, Relatedness) are present at once.

designFeedback.findingTitle: Entry-Level Micro-Rewards: Coins-for-Log (Not Deferred Savings)
designFeedback.findingDescription: Apps that have solved motivation problems do it by making the checking-in behavior immediately rewarding in its own right, rather than as a means to the deferred reward of established habits. Habitica does this by directly connecting task completion to character progression. Rather than rely on "save $X by month end," award small coin micro-rewards (+5 GIL) for each transaction logged or category checked—exactly what Mission Control's quest/XP system already does. Earn coins for completing habit

designFeedback.findingTitle: Category-Coded Donut Chart with Drill-Down Tap
designFeedback.findingDescription: Visual spending breakdowns through a colorful category-based chart make financial data easier to digest. Rather than force users to scan rows, show a donut/ring chart where each color maps to a category (food=#ff8a63, transport=#66c8ff, etc.—reuse Mission Control's palette). Tapping a slice reveals that category's recent transactions below. This taps into immediate pattern recognition and lets users spot overspend at a glance. Pairs well with the hierarchy card above.

designFeedback.findingDescription: When a platform aligns with a user's self-concept, it strengthens intrinsic motivation and persistence. Instead of streaks that punish missing days, Mission Control could reframe daily todo completion as evidence of a chosen identity (e.g., 'organized practitioner', 'focused builder') and highlight *genuine progress toward mastery* via contextual feedback tied to task tags and historical patterns—showing which work modes compound or conflict, what times of day yield depth. This shifts motivation

designFeedback.findingTitle: Responsive Modular Architecture: Bento Hierarchy Scaled for Mobile Native
designFeedback.findingDescription: In 2026, bento box UI moved beyond static landing pages into dashboards, mobile apps, and widget-style system surfaces with interactive states and real-time data making the grid feel alive. Mission Control's mobile 5-tab nav already leans modular; extend this by ensuring card sizes adapt not just to screen size but to content priority. On desktop, the left Todos card dominates (larger area weight); on mobile, each tab becomes a self-contained bento micro-layout (todos ≈ schedule ≈ reminders). Ma

designFeedback.findingTitle: Restraint in Gamification: Motivation via Loss Aversion + Streak Simplicity
designFeedback.findingDescription: Habitica demonstrates that punishment alongside reward (anticipated loss) motivates harder than pure rewards, but apps like Tick Tick prove that minimal gamification (just streaks + a clean counter, no confetti) outperforms feature-heavy systems. Mission Control's rank badges and XP pops already exist; lean into streaks as the primary motivator (visual fill on a calendar tile, color warmth on success), drop cosmetic celebration effects, and reserve rank-ups for genuine difficulty threshol

designFeedback.findingTitle: Consequential Instant Feedback: Haptic + Audio Pulse on Task Completion
designFeedback.findingDescription: When a player checks off a todo or daily habit, Mission Control triggers a millisecond haptic pulse (vibration on mobile, controller rumble on desktop) paired with a crisp, brief chime—creating instant, multi-sensory confirmation that the action *landed*. This makes task completion feel earned and consequential, not just a visual flourish; the sensation is snappy enough to respect focus while being unmistakable enough to feel rewarding.

designFeedback.findingTitle: Consequential Instant Feedback: Haptic + Audio Pulse on Task Completion
designFeedback.findingDescription: Tapping a habit gives instant XP and gold feedback, making choices feel consequential. Instead of a silent animation, Mission Control's checkbox could trigger a brief haptic pulse (vibration on mobile, rumble on controller-paired desktops) paired with a subtle chime—creating a tactile, multi-sensory reward loop that feels *earned* rather than decorative. The sensation is instantaneous and dismissible, respecting focus while confirming the action unmistakably.

designFeedback.findingTitle: Instant Completion Micro-Interactions with Sequenced Feedback Loops
designFeedback.findingDescription: A single click to mark a task done triggers a choreographed sequence: circle fills with color, a checkmark draws, the task label strikes through, a small burst particle effect fires, then the entire row gently collapses or fades. Instead of a drawer or modal, the feedback happens *inline on the card itself*, keeping the battle-menu focus intact while delivering psychological reinforcement and system status confirmation. Fits Mission Control's rank/XP feedback loop perfectly—each rank completion

designFeedback.findingTitle: Reflective Progress Heatmap Instead of Instant Confetti
designFeedback.findingDescription: Rather than ephemeral animations, adopt a GitHub-style contribution grid where each completed day tiles up on a calendar heatmap—empty tiles create visible gaps that push you to fill them. Mission Control's header could swap its linear streak badge for a compact 7-day or 30-day heatmap (rows of colored boxes), letting the daily completion history tell the story visually without cheap confetti noise. The metric becomes compliance against the plan, not consecutive perfection—missing a day is a dat

designFeedback.findingTitle: Drill-Down Detail Exposure (Progressive Disclosure via Expandable Task Cells)
designFeedback.findingDescription: Essential data presented first with supporting metrics accessible via progressive drill-down that starts with a general overview and then goes into detail, facilitating data prioritization and creating clarity. For Mission Control's daily todos, each task cell shows only rank + title by default; tapping/clicking expands to reveal subtasks, due time, tags, or notes in a bottom-drawer slide or inline toggle. Keeps the grid uncluttered while respecting the JRPG battle-menu aesthetic—UI feels lightw

designFeedback.findingTitle: Streak Confetti Burst on Daily Completion
designFeedback.findingDescription: When the user checks off their first task of the day, trigger a brief 1-second CSS keyframe confetti animation (3–5 particles scaling and fading upward) centered on the streak badge in the header. The effect rewards daily habit closure with instant tactile feedback, reinforcing the JRPG battle-menu aesthetic while borrowing gamification momentum from modern habit trackers. Confetti only fires once per calendar day, preventing fatigue.

designFeedback.findingTitle: Anchor + Supporting Cell Ratio (Bento Hierarchy via Area, Not Just Label)
designFeedback.findingDescription: Every bento has one anchor that wins on size by a clear margin, ideally twice the area of the next cell, and the anchor is where the strongest copy, most important visual, or highest-stakes interaction lives. For Mission Control's daily todos, make the S-rank task an anchor (spanning 2 grid columns + 2 rows), A-ranks as secondary cells (1 col × 1.5 rows), and C-rank routine items as minimal supporting cells (1 col × 0.8 rows). This ratio mirrors the visual hierarchy the rest of the page uses, co

designFeedback.findingTitle: Tap-to-Log Quick Action (Finch / Productive Pattern)
designFeedback.findingDescription: Apps like Finch use a cozy, supportive interface for tracking daily goals, making productivity feel gentle rather than demanding. Add a floating "log today" button or a prominent quick-tap region at the bottom of the daily todo list that pre-fills today's date and opens a minimal modal (rank + title only). The best habit tracking apps offer a seamless habits setup process, making sure users log habits fast, reducing friction vs. the current three-step add flow.

designFeedback.findingTitle: Streaks with Confetti Micro-Animation on Daily Mark
designFeedback.findingDescription: Subtle micro animations and visual feedback like confetti explosions reward user actions in real-time. Mission Control has a static streak counter. Add a brief 1-second confetti burst (via CSS keyframes) when a user checks off today's first/final task, triggering only on the streak badge itself. Habit trackers now commonly feature confetti animations and Android support, and retro JRPG menus pair well with particle effects.

designFeedback.findingTitle: Difficulty Signaling via Visual Layering (Bento Grid Weight)
designFeedback.findingDescription: Bento grid is an information architecture decision that controls cognitive load by giving each piece of data its own spatial weight. Apply this to daily todos: bigger/taller cards for high-rank (S/A) tasks, compact rows for routine (C) ones. This mirrors how a hero tile spanning 6 columns creates visual hierarchy through spatial weight so the bigger tile appears more important—letting users visually triage at a glance without text labels.

designFeedback.findingTitle: Tap-to-Log Quick Action (Finch / Productive Pattern)
designFeedback.findingDescription: Apps like Finch use a cozy, supportive interface for tracking daily goals, making productivity feel gentle rather than demanding. Add a floating "log today" button or a prominent quick-tap region at the bottom of the daily todo list that pre-fills today's date and opens a minimal modal (rank + title only). The best habit tracking apps offer a seamless habits setup process, making sure users log habits fast, reducing friction vs. the current three-step add flow.

designFeedback.findingTitle: Streaks with Confetti Micro-Animation on Daily Mark
designFeedback.findingDescription: Subtle micro animations and visual feedback like confetti explosions reward user actions in real-time. Mission Control has a static streak counter. Add a brief 1-second confetti burst (via CSS keyframes) when a user checks off today's first/final task, triggering only on the streak badge itself. Habit trackers now commonly feature confetti animations and Android support, and retro JRPG menus pair well with particle effects.

designFeedback.findingTitle: Difficulty Signaling via Visual Layering (Bento Grid Weight)
designFeedback.findingDescription: Bento grid is an information architecture decision that controls cognitive load by giving each piece of data its own spatial weight. Apply this to daily todos: bigger/taller cards for high-rank (S/A) tasks, compact rows for routine (C) ones. This mirrors how a hero tile spanning 6 columns creates visual hierarchy through spatial weight so the bigger tile appears more important—letting users visually triage at a glance without text labels.

designFeedback.findingTitle: Quality Over Volume (Task Weighting)
designFeedback.findingDescription: Karma rewards task completion regardless of task importance, which means the fastest path to a higher score is completing a high volume of small, easy tasks rather than fewer, meaningful ones. Users who discover this optimize for it, and the inbox fills with two-minute items, important projects sit untouched, and the Karma number climbs while actual productivity declines. designFeedback.findingTitle: Immediate Visual Feedback on Task Completion
designFeedback.findingDescription: The core of the experience is the visual feedback loop. When a user marks a habit as complete, the app must acknowledge it—instantly and satisfyingly. This doesn't mean over-the-top fireworks, but a clear, immediate confirmation that their effort has been recorded. Mission Control already does this well with XP pop animations; enhancing it with a color pulse or rank-check notification (e.g., "S-rank locked" at task completion) would deepen the JRPG feel.

designFeedback.findingTitle: Streak Forgiveness (Grace Days & Freezes)
designFeedback.findingDescription: Streak forgiveness (freezes, grace days, pause buttons) went from premium feature to baseline expectation, driven by the fact that an unforgiving streak breaks once and then breaks forever, because the psychological cost of restarting from zero is heavier than the cost of skipping today. Mission Control could let players "freeze" one day per week without losing their XP streak, or offer a monthly streak-reset token—keeping the JRPG rank feel while staying psychologically forgiving.

thread-1786508871900-0-cognitive-load-re.description: Modern dashboards lean on breathing room and clear content hierarchy rather than cramming every pixel. Instead of showing all todos/reminders at once, use whitespace as a design tool—enlarge primary content blocks (anchor cards), shrink secondary info, and let empty space guide eye flow. This pairs naturally with Mission Control's existing bento structure: make the current 'Todos' card larger (span 2 rows), reduce reminder detail in the right panel, and reserve micro-interactions (XP pops, rank badges) as earned attention-getters, not defaults.

thread-1786508871900-1-restraint-in-gami.description: The gamified productivity category is converging with identity design — not task counts but skill proof. Mission Control could show "competence anchors" (time-of-day proficiency, task-mode synergies, depth vs. speed trade-offs) as contextual mastery evidence tied to historical patterns, replacing generic streak punishment. Systems with great Competence but no Autonomy create a golden cage; the magic happens when all three (Competence, Autonomy, Relatedness) are present at once.

thread-1786508871900-2-responsive-modula.description: Reveal-on-scroll surfaces secondary details as the user scrolls through each section rather than exposing all data upfront, reducing initial cognitive load while preserving power-user depth. Applied to Mission Control: todos show only rank + checkbox initially; scroll reveals XP values and edit affordances. On mobile tabs, each section (tasks, schedule, reminders) hides metadata until scroll, creating a natural funnel from headline to detail without tab proliferation or modal sprawl.

This F-pattern scanning guides attention without labels, letting users grasp financial health in under 5 seconds. Apply to Mission Control's GIL WALLET: make the month's budget total a 2-column card, shrink daily/weekly totals to 1-column tiles, and nest category breakdown (food, transport, etc.) as mini-cards within the grid flow. Reduces scan time and the feeling of 'too much data'.

thread-1786517286745-0-event-driven-soft.title: Event-Driven Soft Refresh with Connection Status Badge
thread-1786517286745-0-event-driven-soft.description: Detect when data arrives and trigger a refresh only when needed, rather than constant polling. When Red finishes a revision, the server emits a lightweight event; the client polls short intervals only while the slideshow modal is open. A small "●" badge in the modal header animates to signal the refresh is live, never blocking the user's view of the current slide. Pairs well with Mission Control's retro aesthetic via simple dot/pulse animations in the accent color.

The iframe mockup beneath cross-fades rather than reloading, preserving scroll position so readers mid-inspection don't lose their place. This creates a sense of seamless update without jolting the viewer—alive but restrained, fitting the JRPG aesthetic of gradual state shifts.

thread-1786517286746-2-pause-on-interact.title: Pause-on-Interact with Manual Refresh Fallback
thread-1786517286746-2-pause-on-interact.description: Provide flexibility: if you're investigating a specific data point and don't want visuals to change, pause live refresh. While paused, no automated refreshes occur; when ready, resume to return to real-time monitoring. A small pause button (⏸) in the slideshow footer stops incoming revisions mid-read; tapping resume or navigating to the next finding auto-restarts polling. Prevents frustration when user is comparing the old mockup to feedback notes. Low-friction, respects user agency—very on-brand for a personal dashboard.

thread-1787674819824-1-predictive-feedba.title: Predictive Feedback Over Reactive Points (Leading Indicators)
thread-1787674819824-1-predictive-feedba.description: Research shows gamified apps see 52% Day-30 dropout, primarily due to novelty fade and external-motivation dependency. Habit formation takes 66+ days; apps that show users what they *can still influence today* (leading indicators like 'complete 2 more quests for streak bonus' or 'aim for 3 S-ranks this week') retain 17% better than apps showing only past completions. This reframes Mission Control's XP system from transaction-feedback to trajectory feedback, keeping motivation intrinsic rather than point-dependent.

thread-1787674819824-2-neumorphic-depth-.title: Neumorphic Depth as Affordance Layer (Not Decoration)
thread-1787674819824-2-neumorphic-depth-.description: Retro-gaming UI and modern dashboard design are converging on neumorphism used solely for interactive affordance—not visual flourish. Soft shadow-highlights on buttons, toggles, and clickable cards signal 'tap me' without bloating contrast or breaking accessibility. Mission Control's JRPG borders already use hard shadows; adding subtle inner-shadow depth to quest checkboxes and time-wheel tiles grounds interactivity in tactile feedback cues, making the UI feel responsive without abandoning the existing dark cyan aesthetic.

designArchive.title: Rank-Locked Celebration Bursts with Staggered Easing Curves
designArchive.description: Asana's task completion uses celebratory animations featuring unexpected reward sequences that make routine achievements feel special. For Mission Control's rank system, apply staggered easing curves per rank (linear for C, ease-out for B, spring overshoot for A/S) so each rank tier *feels* heavier and more rewarding. Circle fills with timed color transition, checkmark draws with stroke animation, label strikes through, then a burst of particles in the rank's own color, before the row gently collapses. Most micro-animations live in the 200–400ms range — cluster fill (0ms) → check (80ms) → strike (120ms) → confetti (200ms) → collapse (600ms).

designArchive.title: Single-Tap Affordance Toggles: Friction-Free Task Completion
designArchive.description: Since a 20-second delay can break automatic behavior and small amounts of friction often beat motivation, Mission Control's todos should support instant checkbox affordance via a single, oversized tap zone per task—no modal, no confirmation, just state-change haptic + color shift. Reducing friction by minimizing steps keeps the daily ritual effortless and habitual, making logging feel automatic rather than ceremonial.

designArchive.description: 2026 dashboard design centers on reducing cognitive overload by showing only what's relevant now. Mission Control could add a simple toggle—e.g., 'Focus Mode' that hides the calendar and weekly schedule, leaving only today's todos and reminders. Alternatively, a 'Dashboard' mode that hides all-day todos and surfaces only upcoming events within 4 hours. This follows the principle that every element should support current decision-making, lowering friction for quick check-ins while keeping full power for deep planning.

designArchive.title: Progressive Disclosure for Daily Todos
designArchive.description: Progressive disclosure shows only essential information upfront and reveals details when needed, simplifying the interface and improving focus. For Mission Control, this means collapsing lower-priority todos by default (C/B ranks shown compact, S/A expanded), unfolding rank badges, XP values, and time estimates only on hover or tap. Reduces cognitive load on first glance while keeping power users' full data a gesture away—fits the JRPG battle-menu vibe of toggling menu depth.

designArchive.description: 2026 trends shift from simple gestures (swipe, tap, pinch) to compound gestures with distinct haptic feedback, so users' thumbs know what they triggered before eyes confirm it. For Mission Control, map swipe-right-to-complete, swipe-left-to-reschedule, long-press-for-details on each todo item. Pair with the existing XP pop animation and scanline flicker to reinforce feedback—turns checkbox interaction into a tactile, game-like moment that feels rewarding and fast.

designArchive.title: Hierarchical Bento Layout to Isolate Todos from Calendar
designArchive.description: Bento grids encode hierarchy directly into layout structure—a card spanning two columns and two rows signals greater importance than single-unit neighbors. Currently Mission Control's three-column grid (todos | schedule | reminders) competes visually. Redesign as a 2×2 bento with a tall hero "Today's Todos" card (left, double-height), a smaller "Calendar Peek" widget (top-right), and reminders/streak counter (bottom-right). Visually separates the daily task focus from calendar clutter while keeping reminders visible. Fits the existing bento-card aesthetic.

designArchive.description: Calendar interfaces can overlay heatmaps showing financial or contextual performance alongside event scheduling, giving users both scheduling and strategic overviews at a glance. For Mission Control, this means toggling between a standard monthly grid and a heatmap showing XP earned per day, task completion density, or event-kind frequency. Mission Control's rank colors (S/A/B/C) and event kind chips already support this visual layering. A heatmap toggle in the calendar modal lets players see patterns at a glance.

designArchive.title: Tile-Based Streak Grid (Gamification via Color, Not Just Numbers)
designArchive.description: Habit trackers using tile-based grids make tracking visually intuitive and satisfying, transforming habit tracking into an engaging experience. Apps like HabitBull visualize streaks by highlighting successful days in green and missed days in pink, acknowledging that life can interfere with streaks while still providing a positive overall view. Mission Control's event-kind chips (training/meeting/focus/social/errand/routine) could fill calendar cells with color blocks instead of text event titles, making a full month of colored tiles feel like filling a progress grid—pure visual satisfaction.

designArchive.title: Overflow Management with '+N More' Popovers & Expand Toggle
designArchive.description: The standard calendar overflow approach shows 2–3 events with a '+N more' indicator—clicking it reveals a popover or expands the cell. Mission Control's current monthly grid already hints at event overflow; implementing a popover for dense days lets high-activity calendars remain scannable while hiding nothing. Event styling should communicate category and duration through color and icons, especially in high-density calendars where color-coding must include pattern or icon differentiation for color-blind users.
designArchive.runTitle: Calendar Upgrades & Gamification for Mission Control

designArchive.title: One-Tap Habit Widget (Zero-Friction Completion)
designArchive.description: Habit trackers like Loop Habit Tracker and HabitHub succeed by letting users mark habits done directly from the home screen widget in one tap, saving 20–30 seconds per habit per day. Mission Control could surface today's highest-priority todos (rank S/A) as a dedicated widget card that toggles completion state without opening the full dashboard. Pairs with the existing rank/XP system and keeps the home tab focused on immediate action.
designArchive.runTitle: Mobile Widget Interaction & Retro Gamification in Personal Dashboards

designArchive.title: Claymorphism Touch on Retro Grid (Tactile Neumorphism for Gaming UI)
designArchive.description: 2025–26 design trends show claymorphism (soft 3D, friendlier than neumorphism) pairs beautifully with retro gaming aesthetics—Press Start microtrend merges '70s–'80s pixel art with neon and tech-inspired visuals. Mission Control already uses inset shadows and bold colors; replacing hard shadows with softer, rounded 3D-effect tiles on the mobile home tab (todos, reminders, schedule widgets) would feel more tactile and 'playable' while honoring the JRPG identity.
designArchive.runTitle: Mobile Widget Interaction & Retro Gamification in Personal Dashboards

designArchive.title: Asymmetric Bento Grid for Mobile (Spatial Priority Signaling)
designArchive.description: Bento grids (variable-size tiles in CSS Grid) communicate data priority through spatial weight alone—larger tiles draw eyes first. Perfect for Mission Control's mobile home tab: make today's rank-S todos span 2 columns, reminders 1 column, and the weekly bar full-width below. No badge inflation needed; the grid layout does the hierarchy. Reduces cognitive load on small screens and scales cleanly across devices.
designArchive.runTitle: Mobile Widget Interaction & Retro Gamification in Personal Dashboards

designArchive.title: Cognitive Load Zones – Progressive Information Reveal
designArchive.description: <cite index="3-12">Accessible dashboards must design for cognitive load, removing elements that don't support the user's current decision</cite>. Mission Control's three-column layout is strong, but the weekly schedule expansion toggle could be enhanced with a "progressive disclosure" approach: show only today's + tomorrow's events by default, expand on-demand. <cite index="16-8">Bento grids control cognitive load by giving each piece of data its own spatial weight</cite>. Apply this to reminders: group by time-until-due (due today, due this week, due later) rather than flat chronology.
designArchive.runTitle: Dashboard Clarity & Gamification Engagement

designArchive.title: Weekend Gamification Anchor – Weekly Challenge Reset
designArchive.description: <cite index="9-5,9-6">Productivity app streaks break 25% more on Fridays because external work structure disappears, and the habit fails completely at weekends</cite>. Mission Control already seeds weekly Pokémon every Monday, which is strong. Enhance this: add a "Weekend Quest" mode that unlocks Friday afternoon—goals shift from work-focused (training, meeting) to personal (social, routine) with reduced XP thresholds, and a "Comeback Bonus" if streaks resume Monday. This uses gamification's documented ability to <cite index="8-7">transform routine activities into experiences users actively want to complete</cite>.
designArchive.runTitle: Dashboard Clarity & Gamification Engagement

designArchive.title: Metric Gaming Prevention – Outcome-Over-Volume Reward
designArchive.description: <cite index="9-17,9-18">Points systems work for productivity when they reward the right actions, not actions optimized for the metric itself</cite>. Mission Control's rank system (S/A/B/C with fixed XP per rank) is clean but rewards task completion count equally regardless of effort. Consider a "depth badge": if a task stays marked as in-progress for >2 hours (indicating focus work), award +2 XP; if finished in <10 minutes, award +1. <cite index="8-9,8-10,8-11">Visibility of progress is powerful for long-term goals, but learning/habits rarely deliver immediate results</cite>. The depth metric makes focus visible and rewards concentration, not speed.
